templates.name: Triple Lock: Face + Outfit + Scene
templates.description: Three references, each locking one thing — who, what they wear, where they are.
templates.useCase: The most controlled composite Studio can do. Separating identity, wardrobe and location into their own references stops the model trading one off against another — the usual failure where a new outfit quietly changes the face.

data.label: Master Composition
data.text:
# MASTER REFERENCE COMPOSITION — IDENTITY LOCK + OUTFIT LOCK + SCENE LOCK

IMAGE 01 = IDENTITY. Use this face only: same bone structure, eyes, brows, nose, lips, skin tone and hair. Do not beautify, slim, age or restyle the face.

IMAGE 02 = OUTFIT. Reproduce every garment and accessory exactly as shown — cut, colour, print placement, fabric, footwear and bag. No substitutions.

IMAGE 03 = SCENE. Place her in this exact location, matching its perspective, lighting direction, colour temperature and depth of field.

OUTPUT: full-body shot of the IMAGE 01 person wearing the IMAGE 02 outfit inside the IMAGE 03 scene. Photographic, natural light, sharp on the subject.

data.label: Motion Prompt

Use the reference image as the ONLY visual source for the person, outfit and location.

data.label: Master Composition
data.text:
# ROLE ORDER — read the references in this exact order

IMAGE 01 = FACE. Facial identity source only. Same bone structure, eyes, brows, nose, lips, skin tone and hair. Do not beautify, slim or restyle the face.

IMAGE 02 = OUTFIT. Wardrobe source only. Reproduce each garment exactly — cut, colour, knit texture, layering and footwear. Ignore the body and background of this image.

IMAGE 03 = PRODUCT + SETTING. The product must match this photo exactly: same silhouette, upholstery colour, stitching, armrests, base and castors. Keep the room, window light and desk as shown. Do not redesign the product.

OUTPUT: the IMAGE 01 woman, wearing the IMAGE 02 outfit, seated naturally in the IMAGE 03 product within that room. Full body visible, photographic, daylight from the window.

templates.name: Exercise Series: 1 Mascot → 4 Clips
templates.description: One character reference becomes four storyboards, then four 10-second vertical clips.
templates.useCase: Faceless fitness and how-to channels. Four parallel branches from a single style reference, so a whole series shares one look — and storyboarding before animating means you approve the movement while it is still cheap to change.

data.label: Push-Up — Storyboard
data.text:
Use the attached reference image as the visual style guide.

# COMMON STYLE CONSTANTS — identical in every frame
• Same character: faceless golden-yellow figure, heavy black outlines, flat vector
  shading, dark grey shorts, one dark grey arm sleeve
• Same dark neutral background and lighting
• Same body proportions and muscle definition — do not restyle or re-anatomise

# OUTPUT — a 2x2 storyboard grid of one full push-up repetition, labelled FRAME 01 to FRAME 04
FRAME 01 — high plank, arms extended, body in a straight line
FRAME 02 — lowering, elbows tracking back at 45°
FRAME 03 — bottom position, chest just above the floor
FRAME 04 — pressing back up to the start

Tint the muscles doing the work in a brighter yellow in each frame. Keep the four panels the same scale and camera distance so they read as one sequence.

data.label: Push-Up — Motion
data.text:
Create a 10-second vertical animated clip from the uploaded storyboard.

Follow FRAME 01 → 04 in order as the motion path, looping smoothly back to the start. Keep the character exactly as shown — same golden-yellow figure, black outlines, flat vector style, dark shorts and sleeve, same background. Continuous motion, no morphing, no style drift, no camera cuts. Vertical 9:16 framing.

templates.name: ASMR Styrofoam Carving: 6-Clip Chain
templates.description: One reference photo becomes a six-clip carving sequence, with every handoff frame shown on the canvas.
templates.useCase: ASMR and satisfying-craft channels. This is the format people usually build by hand — generate a clip, screenshot its last frame, upload it as the next clip's first frame, repeat five times. Studio passes each clip's closing frame to the next node automatically, so the block genuinely progresses from raw foam to finished sculpture in one run.

data.label: 1. Measuring & Cutting
data.text:
Hands measure a white styrofoam sheet with a steel ruler, mark cut lines in pencil, then draw a utility knife through the foam in slow even passes. Linger on the blade parting the surface and the crumbs dropping away.
END ON: several clean rectangular blocks squared up in a neat stack.

# SUBJECT
Carve the subject in the attached reference image — match its shape, proportions and details closely. If no reference is attached, carve a seated lion. This format reads best with animals that have a strong silhouette.

# CONSTANTS — identical in every clip
• Macro close-ups at bench level, three-quarter view, so the form stays readable. Top-down only while measuring and cutting flat stock.
• Hands and forearms visible, never a face.
• Same warm workshop lighting, same worn wooden bench, tools and a jar of brushes soft and out of focus behind.
• Photoreal materials: white foam grain, static-clinging dust, blade marks, loose crumbs and offcuts scattered across the bench.
• ASMR audio led by the tools — blade shearing foam, dry crumbling, sanding grit.
• Unhurried, steady hands. One continuous take, no cuts, no time-lapse.
• Vertical 9:16, high detail.

data.label: 2. Stacking & Bonding
data.text:
White glue is spread across each block face, the blocks are pressed together one by one and squared into a single tall cube. Show the glue squeezing out at the seams and hands holding steady pressure.
END ON: one solid bonded cube resting on the bench, seams barely visible.

templates.name: Emotional Short: 1 Character → 10 Beats
templates.description: Tension, escalation, an unexpected kindness, relief — ten scenes holding one character.
templates.useCase: The retention format: cold open on trouble, escalate, turn on an act of kindness, resolve warm — and frame the last shot to match the first so it loops. Every scene references the character sheet rather than the scene before it, because these are ten different moments and a face that drifts in scene 3 would otherwise poison the seven after it. The colour arc is the part most people skip and it does real work: desaturated blue-grey through the tense half, warming to gold at the turn. Ten 8s clips give you the spine, not the finished film — the 2-4 second cutting the format lives on happens in the edit, where you cover each beat from more than one angle.

data.label: Character Design
data.text:
Character reference sheet: one photorealistic 3D animated character, on a plain mid-grey backdrop.

A boy of about ten, thin, with dark tousled hair and large expressive brown eyes. Wearing a faded oversized green jacket with frayed cuffs, a grey shirt and worn trainers. Carrying a canvas satchel across one shoulder.

Three views: three-quarter front on the left, side profile in the centre, three-quarter back on the right. Neutral even lighting, full body, sharp focus, natural skin and fabric texture.

An original fictional character, not any real person.

data.label: 1. Hook — Something Is Wrong
data.text:
The boy stands alone at the mouth of a rain-soaked alley at dusk, clutching his satchel to his chest, looking back over his shoulder at something out of frame. Rain streaks the air. He is breathing fast.
COLOUR: desaturated blue-grey, cold, heavy shadows. Open on his face.

Ultra-realistic 3D animation, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, 35mm feel. Rendered like a modern animated feature, not a game engine.
Same character as the reference: identical face, hair, build, clothing and colour palette. Do not restyle, age or redesign them.
Expression carries the scene — the story is told in faces and body language, not dialogue. No spoken lines, no on-screen text, no subtitles.
One continuous shot, no cuts inside the clip. Slow deliberate camera.
Vertical 9:16.

templates.name: Miniature Car: Carve → Match Cut
templates.description: Name a car. Flow draws the reference sheet, then four clips carve it and match-cut to the real one.
templates.useCase: The build-up-and-reveal format, where the whole video is a setup for the last two seconds. Change the first line of the first node to any car — "BMW M3 E46, 2003, Laguna Seca Blue" — and it renders a three-view reference sheet, then carves it, details it, paints it and reveals it full size. No photo to source, and the sheet comes out at the angles and lighting the carve clips need rather than whatever a stock shot happened to be. The Last Frame nodes matter more here than anywhere: the match cut only lands if the miniature the reveal inherits is exactly the one the previous clip finished, so the handoff sits on the canvas where you can check it before spending a generation. Editing note from the format — post the reveal first as the hook, then the build.

templates.name: Water Wipeouts: 4 Written by AI
templates.description: ChatGPT writes four different wipeout prompts, Flow renders all four — a different set every run.
templates.useCase: Faceless fail and satisfying channels, where the format never changes but the clip has to. One brief fans out to four Ask AI nodes, and because they run as consecutive turns in the same ChatGPT conversation each one is told to differ from the last — so a single Run gives four unrelated wipeouts. Needs a signed-in ChatGPT tab; clips are 10s, which is Flow's longest.

data.label: The Brief
data.text:
Write ONE prompt for a 10-second vertical AI video. Output only the prompt itself — no title, no explanation, no preamble, no quotes, no markdown.

# THE SHOT
A single contestant attempting a floating obstacle course over water, filmed by a friend on a modern phone. One continuous handheld take, no cuts. The contestant's face stays visible. It ends in one unexpected wipeout.

# MUST READ AS A REAL PHONE VIDEO
• Handheld from the poolside, slight micro-shake, imperfect framing, a touch of autofocus hunting.
• Never drone, tripod, gimbal, stabiliser or cinematic camera moves.
• The person filming is never seen — no hands, shadow or reflection.
• Natural sound only: splashes, wet slaps on inflatables, shouting, laughing, pool ambience. No music, no narration.
• Nothing glossy — not an advert, not influencer content, not a film.

# VARY IT
Pick a different location, contestant and obstacle order than any prompt you have already written in this conversation, and end on a different wipeout. Obstacles to draw from: floating pads, balance beam, rolling log, rope swing, tilting platform, rotating arm, slippery ramp, foam wall.

# BEAT-BY-BEAT
Describe the ten seconds in order — the approach, two or three obstacles, then the fall. Keep it under 150 words.
